items.titleJp: 市民[しみん]スポーツセンター プール休館[きゅうかん]のお知[し]らせ

Please note that the 2nd-floor training room and gymnasium remain open as usual from 9:00 AM to 9:00 PM. Pool members may use the training room free of charge during this period only.

items.titleJp: 先輩[せんぱい]への教科書[きょうかしょ]のお願[ねが]い
items.titleEn: Borrowing a Textbook from a Senior

items.titleJp: ベランダで始[はじ]めた野菜[やさい]づくり

translationEn: This spring, I started growing cherry tomatoes on my small apartment balcony. Buying them at the supermarket might be cheaper, but I wanted to try growing them myself.

Watering them first thing every morning and checking the leaves became something I look forward to. At first, bugs got on them and I was worried, but after looking up remedies in a book and taking action, they became healthy again.
Last week, I finally harvested three red tomatoes. They were a little small, yet they were very sweet and I was deeply moved.

items.titleJp: 手書[てが]きの手紙[てがみ]がうれしい理由[りゆう]
items.contextEn: Short reflective essay on digital messaging versus handwritten letters.
paragraphs: スマートフォンを使[つか]えば、どんなに遠[とお]くにいる友達[ともだち]にも一秒[いちびょう]でメッセージを送[おく]ることができる。とても便利[べんり]で、私[わたし]も毎日[まいにち]使[つか]っている。

translationEn: With a smartphone, you can send a message in one second to a friend no matter how far away they are. It is very convenient, and I use it every day too.

However, the other day, when a birthday postcard arrived from my grandmother, I felt a warmth that cannot be felt on a smartphone. Looking at the characters written carefully one by one conveys that she spent time for me.
Text messages are plenty for urgent communication, yet when you want to express important gratitude, I think it is worth sending something handwritten even if it takes effort.

questions.explanationEn: Paragraph 2 explains that seeing the carefully written letters conveys that her grandmother spent time for her.

questions.explanationEn: Paragraph 3 states digital messages are fine for urgent matters, while handwritten notes are worth the effort for important gratitude.

items.titleJp: 初[はじ]めての新幹線[しんかんせん]
items.titleEn: Riding the Shinkansen for the First Time
items.contextEn: Short travel essay by an exchange student riding the bullet train.
paragraphs: 先週[せんしゅう]の土曜日[どようび]、初[はじ]めて新幹線[しんかんせん]に乗[の]って大阪[おおさか]へ行[い]きました。出発[しゅっぱつ]の前[まえ]に駅[えき]で駅弁[えきべん]とお茶[ちゃ]を買[か]いました。
新幹線[しんかんせん]はとても速[はや]いのに、中[なか]は思[おも]っていたよりずっと静[しず]かで、ほとんど揺[ゆ]れませんでした。窓側[まどがわ]の席[せき]を予約[よやく]しておいたので、晴[は]れた空[そら]の下[した]に富士山[ふじさん]をはっきり見[み]ることができました。

translationEn: Last Saturday, I rode the Shinkansen for the first time to go to Osaka. Before departure, I bought a station bento box and tea at the station.

Even though the Shinkansen is very fast, the inside was much quieter than I had expected and barely shook at all. Because I had reserved a window seat in advance, I was able to clearly see Mount Fuji under the clear sky.
Compared to airplanes, you do not need time to get to the airport, so I felt the Shinkansen is very convenient between Tokyo and Osaka.

questions.explanationEn: Paragraph 3 states that compared to flying, you do not need time to travel to the airport (空港まで行く時間がいらないので).
